root.title: Human Readable
root.gist: Two stories argue that networks too complex for humans to understand inevitably get gamed by the powerful, so people need the right to interrogate them.
root.question: Human-readable networks — why must opaque, self-organizing systems remain accountable to the people they serve? (two linked stories)

children.title: 1. Nice networks don't go down
children.gist: When the ant-like routing network that runs all traffic crashes, a couple navigates an old phone and a map to reach a family ceremony, where Trish becomes a hero by saving two drowning swimmers.
children.question: The first Downtime — how does a sudden network failure test the couple and reveal what the invisible system actually controls? (a date-day narrative)

children.title: The grid fails mid-date
children.gist: Nineteen seconds into catastrophic failure the ant-routed traffic network stills every car and screen, stranding Trish and Rainer on the Interstate on their eighth date.

children.title: Manual navigation
children.gist: Lacking any digital routing, the couple improvises with a paper map and an old-fashioned phone, bantering their way into getting usable directions from Rainer's mother.

children.title: The unveiling explained
children.gist: Driving on through eerily stalled traffic, Rainer explains the Jewish mourning rituals and tombstone unveiling his family practices, comparing religious law to the ants' routing rules people trust without understanding.

children.title: Meeting the family
children.gist: At the cemetery Trish meets Rainer's mother and extended family, improvising mourning-pebbles from a smashed phone and getting absorbed into the clan's warm chaos.

children.title: The rescue
children.gist: At the after-gathering a widow confides in Trish just before two swimmers start drowning, prompting Trish to strip down and use her lifeguard training to pull a boy and a surfer from the sea.

children.title: Driving home through the blackout
children.gist: Returning through a Los Angeles crippled by fires and gridlock without its routing network, the exhausted pair finally relax together, though Rainer's declaration of love breaks their dating rules.

children.title: 2. Progress pilgrims
children.gist: News of the Downtime's human cost, including the surfer's death, pushes Trish to quit academia and lead a new group demanding that emergent networks be made accountable to the people who depend on them.
children.question: Human-Readable World's founding — why does Trish decide the ant-routed network's hidden unfairness must be exposed and regulated? (an origin account)

children.title: Watching the pundits
children.gist: While the network slowly reboots, Trish and Rainer watch televised experts debate whether ant-colony-style routing can go wrong, foreshadowing the fight to come between them.

children.title: The surfer's death
children.gist: Trish learns by email that the surfer she rescued has died, and Rainer comforts her through grief that is tangled up with guilt over a system failure no one could explain.

children.title: Choosing Washington
children.gist: Trish takes a job leading the Association for a Human-Readable World, explaining to Rainer that the network's hidden routing favors the rich and needs transparency and accountability like any other power.

children.title: Opposing arguments laid out
children.gist: In their final conversation as a couple, Rainer insists the network is mathematically incorruptible while Trish maintains that unequal outcomes prove otherwise, and they part as professional rivals who still care for each other.

children.title: 3. Conflict of Insect
children.gist: As Trish's bill to regulate the network battles Rainer's industry lobby through one political setback after another, a second catastrophic Downtime finally forces compromise, reuniting them on uncertain terms.
children.question: The human-readable bill's fight — how does a second network collapse finally break the deadlock between Trish and Rainer's sides? (a legislative battle)

children.title: Rallying the staff
children.gist: Trish pep-talks her small, underfunded team through dirty tricks apparently aimed at her campaign, comparing their fight to Gandhi's path from ridicule to victory.

children.title: Reunion as rivals
children.gist: Trish and Rainer meet again professionally, now representing opposing industry and advocacy interests, and their old intimacy collides awkwardly with Washington's strict rules about meetings and motives.

children.title: The bill's slow progress
children.gist: Despite committee maneuvering and sabotage that mysteriously targets her office's communications, Trish gets her bill introduced, scoring an early win against Rainer's well-funded industry association.

children.title: Televised debate
children.gist: On live television Trish and Rainer spar over whether invisible networks secretly favor the powerful, trading barbed arguments about liberty, efficiency, and who gets to question the system.

children.title: The second Downtime
children.gist: A catastrophic eight-day nationwide outage kills people and cripples institutions, suddenly making everyone eager to listen to Trish's warnings about unaccountable, ungoverned infrastructure.

children.title: Forcing compromise
children.gist: Amid the crisis Rainer, having lost his job, pleads for Trish's help, and together they draft emergency bipartisan language that finally pushes the bill through both chambers of Congress.

children.title: An uneasy ending
children.gist: After the bill passes, Rainer shows up unemployed and hopeful for reconciliation, but Trish, drawn back to her career and unwilling to abandon it, sends him away still divided by their differing faiths in the system.

children.title: Afterword to Human Readable
children.gist: The author's note on writing the story for his then-girlfriend, crediting the real research on ant-colony optimization and legible computing that inspired its central tension.

children.title: Liberation Spectrum
children.gist: A mobile cognitive-radio startup wiring Native reservations with unlicensed wireless networks nearly collapses under an investor coup and a violent standoff, until its founder forces his way back into control.
children.question: CogRad's crisis — why does a founder lose, then reclaim, control of the company he built to bring uncontrolled radio networks to reservations? (a workplace power struggle)

children.title: Life on the road
children.gist: CogRad's traveling multinational of technicians crosses into the US exhausted, its culture of rough camaraderie and commercialized roadhouse stops shown through founder Lee-Daniel's weary leadership.

children.title: Investors move against the founder
children.gist: Lee-Daniel's angel investor Mac reveals that the board intends to replace him with a seasoned executive now that the ad-hoc, unlicensed wireless business must professionalize and expand abroad.

children.title: Winning over the Mohawk Warriors
children.gist: On the Akwesahsne reservation Lee-Daniel's crew earns the wary Mohawk Warriors' trust by teaching surveying skills and respecting strict rules protecting sacred land from the radio installation.

children.title: The ultimatum
children.gist: Cornered by investors demanding he accept a demotion or firing, Lee-Daniel stalls for half an hour alone to find leverage before the deal can be forced on him.

children.title: Firing the crew
children.gist: Lee-Daniel secretly tells his loyal lieutenant that the investors plan to fire most of the staff, triggering a ceremonial ritual ride-along that turns tense as word quietly spreads.

children.title: Standoff in the woods
children.gist: A perimeter survey walk turns into an armed confrontation with Quebec provincial police, forcing Lee-Daniel's crew to flee through the forest while he surrenders to protect his investors.

children.title: Chaos and leverage
children.gist: Back at the bus, a drunken employee revolt and looting spree gives Lee-Daniel the leverage to demand the investors sell him their stakes back within minutes rather than lose everything.

children.title: Afterword to Liberation Spectrum
children.gist: The author's note on writing the story for a workshop, crediting inspiration from cognitive-radio research on tribal land and the real Oka standoff between Mohawk Warriors and armed police.
